The United Kingdom of England and Ireland

q: What are the Falkland Islands and St Helena?

q: Where does the UK Parliament sit?

q: What is the capital city of the UK?

q: What is the capital city of Scotland?

q: What is the capital city of Wales?

q: What is the capital city of Northern Ireland?

q: The Channel Islands and the Isle of Man have their own governments.

q: What does the UK flag, the Union Flag, consist of?

Two crosses: St George and St David

The Welsh dragon and three crosses

q: During the Stone Age, Britain was connected to the continent by a land bridge.
e: True — Stone Age hunter-gatherers could walk to and from Europe.

q: About how long ago did Britain become permanently separated from the continent?

q: When did the first farmers arrive in Britain?
e: The first farmers arrived about 6,000 years ago, probably from south-east Europe.

q: Where is Stonehenge?

q: Where is Skara Brae, the best-preserved prehistoric village in northern Europe?
o: Orkney, off the north coast of Scotland
e: Skara Brae is on Orkney, off the north coast of Scotland.

q: During the Bronze Age, how did people bury their dead?
e: Bronze Age people buried their dead in tombs called round barrows.

q: What were hill forts?
o: Iron Age settlements on hills, like Maiden Castle in Dorset
e: Iron Age people built hill forts. Maiden Castle in Dorset is an impressive example.

q: The first coins minted in Britain were made during the Iron Age.

q: In which year did the Roman Emperor Claudius lead the Roman invasion of Britain?

q: Who was Boudicca?
o: Queen of the Iceni, who fought against the Romans
e: Boudicca, queen of the Iceni in what is now eastern England, fought the Romans.

q: Where is there a statue of Boudicca?

q: Why was Hadrian's Wall built?
o: To keep out the Picts (ancestors of the Scottish people)
To mark the border with Wales
e: Emperor Hadrian built the wall in the north of England to keep out the Picts.

q: For about how long did the Romans stay in Britain?
e: The Romans stayed for about 400 years and left in AD 410.

q: When did the Romans leave Britain?
e: The Romans left in AD 410 to defend other parts of their empire.

q: Which TWO things did the Romans bring to Britain?
e: The Romans brought new plants and animals, roads, public buildings and a legal system.

q: Which tribes invaded Britain after the Romans left?
e: The Jutes, Angles and Saxons invaded from northern Europe.

q: What was found at Sutton Hoo in Suffolk?
o: The burial place of an Anglo-Saxon king, buried in a ship with treasure
e: Sutton Hoo was the burial place of an Anglo-Saxon king, buried with treasure and armour in a ship.

q: Who became the first Archbishop of Canterbury?

q: Where did St Columba found a monastery?

q: Who was the patron saint of Ireland who brought Christianity there?

q: When did the Vikings first visit Britain?

q: Which Anglo-Saxon king united the kingdoms and defeated the Vikings?

q: What was the Danelaw?
o: The part of England where the Vikings settled
e: Vikings settled in the east and north of England, an area known as the Danelaw.

q: Who united the people of the north under one king, the beginning of Scotland as a kingdom?
e: Kenneth MacAlpin became king of the Picts and Scots — the start of the kingdom of Scotland.

q: In which year did the Norman Conquest take place?
e: William, Duke of Normandy, defeated King Harold at the Battle of Hastings in 1066.

q: Who did William of Normandy defeat at the Battle of Hastings?
e: William defeated the English king, Harold, who was killed in the battle.

q: What does the Bayeux Tapestry show?
o: The Norman Conquest and the Battle of Hastings
e: The Bayeux Tapestry commemorates the Norman Conquest and can still be seen in France.

q: What was the Domesday Book?
o: A record of towns, villages, people and animals in England, made for William the Conqueror
A record of Black Death victims
e: William the Conqueror had a list made of all the towns and villages — the Domesday Book.

q: The Normans conquered Scotland as well as England.

q: Which king conquered Wales by 1284?

q: Which TWO castles did Edward I build in Wales to keep his power?

q: Which battle in 1314 did the Scots win against the English?

q: Who led the Scots at the Battle of Bannockburn?
e: Robert the Bruce led the Scots to victory in 1314.

q: What was the Hundred Years War?
o: A war between England and France, which actually lasted 116 years
A war between England and Scotland
e: The Hundred Years War with France actually lasted 116 years.

q: Which famous battle did Henry V win in 1415?
e: King Henry V's army defeated the French at Agincourt in 1415.

q: In which year did the Black Death come to Britain?
e: The Black Death, a form of plague, came to Britain in 1348.

q: About how much of the population of England died in the Black Death?
e: About one third of the population of England died.

q: In which year did King John agree to Magna Carta?
e: In 1215 King John was forced to agree to Magna Carta.

q: What did Magna Carta establish?
o: That even the king was subject to the law
That Parliament could choose the king

The House of Kings and the House of Bishops
The Upper Court and the Lower Court

The judges, the lawyers and the police
The farmers, the soldiers and the merchants

q: Who wrote The Canterbury Tales?
e: Geoffrey Chaucer wrote The Canterbury Tales, about pilgrims travelling to Canterbury.

q: Who was the first person in England to print books using a printing press?
e: William Caxton was the first to print books in England.

q: What were the Wars of the Roses?
o: A civil war between the House of Lancaster and the House of York
A war between England and France
A war between Scotland and England

Lancaster a thistle, York a daffodil

q: Which translation of the Bible was produced in the reign of James I?

q: What were the two sides in the English Civil War?

q: Who wrote a famous diary describing the Great Fire of London?

q: What did the Habeas Corpus Act of 1679 guarantee?

q: What happened in the Glorious Revolution of 1688?

q: Who were the Huguenots who came to Britain between 1680 and 1720?

q: When did it become illegal to trade slaves in British ships or ports?

q: Which MP played an important part in ending the slave trade?

q: Where can you see Nelson's ship, HMS Victory?

q: Who defeated Napoleon at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815?

q: What was the Duke of Wellington's nickname?
e: Wellington was known as the Iron Duke.

q: In which year did Ireland join England, Scotland and Wales to form the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland?

q: What is the cross of St George on the Union Flag?

A diagonal white cross on a blue ground

q: What did the Reform Act of 1832 do?

q: What did the Chartists campaign for?

q: Which Victorian engineer built the Great Western Railway?

q: Which bridge in Bristol did Brunel design?

q: Where was the Great Exhibition of 1851 held?
o: In the Crystal Palace in Hyde Park
e: The Great Exhibition was held in the Crystal Palace, a huge glass building in Hyde Park.

q: In which war did Florence Nightingale nurse soldiers?
e: Florence Nightingale and her nurses treated soldiers in the Crimean War.

q: What did Florence Nightingale set up in 1860?
o: The Nightingale Training School for nurses at St Thomas' Hospital
e: She set up the Nightingale Training School for nurses at St Thomas' Hospital in London.

q: What medal for bravery was introduced during the Crimean War?

q: What happened in Ireland in the mid-1840s?
o: A potato famine — a million people died and many emigrated

q: In 1847, what was the limit on working hours for women and children?

q: Before 1870, what happened to a woman's money and property when she married?

q: Who was the leader of the suffragettes?

q: In which year did women over 30 get the right to vote?
e: In 1918 women over 30 got the vote.

q: In which year did women get the right to vote at 21, the same age as men?
e: In 1928 women got the vote at 21, like men.

q: Between which years was the Boer War fought?
e: The Boer War in South Africa was fought from 1899 to 1902.

q: Who wrote "The Jungle Book" and the poem "If"?
e: Rudyard Kipling, born in India, won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1907.

q: When did the First World War begin?

q: What event triggered the First World War?

q: On the first day of the Battle of the Somme in 1916, about how many British casualties were there?

q: What happened in Ireland in 1916?

q: What happened in the 1930s around the world, including in the UK?
o: The Great Depression, with mass unemployment
e: In 1929 the world went into the Great Depression; some parts of the UK had mass unemployment.

q: In which year did the BBC start the world's first regular television service?
e: The BBC started the world's first regular television service in 1936.

q: When did the Second World War begin?

q: Who became Prime Minister in 1940 and led Britain during the Second World War?

q: What happened at Dunkirk in 1940?

The RAF defeated the German air force

q: What was the Battle of Britain?
o: An air battle in the summer of 1940 between the RAF and the German air force
A naval battle in the Channel

q: Which TWO aircraft were flown by the RAF in the Battle of Britain?

q: What was the Blitz?

q: What happened on D-Day, 6 June 1944?

q: When did the war in Europe end?

q: Which famous words did Churchill say in a speech in 1940?
o: We shall fight on the beaches
To be or not to be

q: Which words did Churchill say about the RAF pilots in the Battle of Britain?
o: Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few

e: Churchill praised the RAF pilots with these words.

q: Who discovered penicillin in 1928?

q: What are the two Houses of Parliament?
o: The House of Commons and the House of Lords
The House of Commons and the Senate
The House of Lords and the Supreme Court
The Cabinet and the House of Commons
e: Parliament has two Houses: the House of Commons and the House of Lords.

q: Which House of Parliament is more important, because its members are democratically elected?
e: The House of Commons is the more important chamber because it is elected.

q: What are the people elected to the House of Commons called?
e: Members of the House of Commons are MPs.

q: What is the area each MP represents called?
e: Each MP represents a parliamentary constituency.

q: How many parliamentary constituencies are there in the UK?
e: The UK is divided into 650 constituencies, each with one MP.

q: How often must a general election be held?
e: General elections are held at least every five years.

q: What happens if an MP dies or resigns?
o: A by-election is held for that constituency
The seat stays empty until the next general election
The party chooses a new MP
The monarch appoints a new MP
e: A by-election is held to choose a new MP.

q: What electoral system is used to elect MPs?
o: First past the post — the candidate with the most votes wins
e: MPs are elected by "first past the post": the candidate with the most votes in the constituency wins.

q: What do party whips do?
o: Make sure MPs attend and vote in Parliament
Chair debates in the House of Commons
e: Whips are responsible for discipline in their party and make sure MPs attend votes.

q: Who chairs debates and keeps order in the House of Commons?
e: The Speaker keeps order and makes sure the rules are followed.

q: How is the Speaker of the House of Commons chosen?
o: By other MPs in a secret ballot
e: The Speaker is chosen by other MPs in a secret ballot.

q: The Speaker is politically neutral.
e: True — the Speaker is neutral, though they still represent their constituency as an MP.

q: Members of the House of Lords are elected by the public.
e: False — members of the House of Lords (peers) are not elected by the people.

q: Since 1958, who appoints life peers to the House of Lords?
o: The monarch, on the advice of the Prime Minister
e: Since 1958 the Prime Minister has had the power to nominate life peers, appointed by the monarch.

q: Which TWO groups can sit in the House of Lords?
o: Senior bishops of the Church of England
e: The House of Lords includes life peers, some hereditary peers and senior Church of England bishops.

q: What can the House of Lords do with new laws proposed by the House of Commons?
o: Suggest amendments or propose new laws, which are then discussed by MPs
Cancel any law it does not like
Approve laws only after a public vote
Nothing — it has no role in making laws
e: The Lords can suggest changes and check laws, but the Commons can overrule them.

q: The House of Commons has powers to overrule the House of Lords.
e: True — the elected House of Commons can overrule the Lords, but this is not used often.

q: Where does the Prime Minister live?
e: The Prime Minister's official home is 10 Downing Street in London.

q: What is the name of the Prime Minister's country house?
e: The Prime Minister also has a country house outside London called Chequers.

q: Who is the Prime Minister?
o: The leader of the political party in power
The leader of the largest party in the House of Lords
The person chosen by the monarch from the public
The Speaker of the House of Commons
e: The Prime Minister is the leader of the party in power and appoints the government ministers.

q: What is the Cabinet?
o: A small committee of about 20 senior ministers
All MPs in the governing party
e: The Prime Minister appoints about 20 senior MPs to the Cabinet.

q: Which Cabinet minister is responsible for the economy?
e: The Chancellor of the Exchequer is responsible for the economy.

q: Which Cabinet minister is responsible for crime, policing and immigration?
e: The Home Secretary is responsible for crime, policing and immigration.

q: Which Cabinet minister is responsible for managing relationships with other countries?
e: The Foreign Secretary manages relationships with foreign countries.

q: What is the Official Opposition?
o: The second-largest party in the House of Commons
e: The second-largest party is called the Opposition, and its leader is the Leader of the Opposition.

q: Who does the Leader of the Opposition appoint to speak on each area of policy?
e: The Leader of the Opposition appoints senior opposition MPs to a shadow cabinet.

q: What happens during Prime Minister's Questions?
o: The Leader of the Opposition and other MPs ask the Prime Minister questions
The monarch questions the Prime Minister
e: Prime Minister's Questions takes place every week while Parliament is sitting.

q: How often does Prime Minister's Questions take place while Parliament is sitting?
e: PMQs happens every week while Parliament is sitting.

q: What are pressure and lobby groups?
o: Organisations that try to influence government policy
e: Pressure and lobby groups try to influence government policy.

q: Civil servants are politically neutral.
e: True — civil servants carry out government policy and are chosen on merit, not by political party.

q: Who carries out government policy?
e: Civil servants support the government in developing and carrying out its policies.

q: What is a local council responsible for?
o: Local services such as education, housing, social services, roads and refuse collection
e: Local authorities provide services in their area and are funded by central government and local taxes.

q: When are most local elections held?
e: Most local authority elections are held in May every year.

q: Some towns and cities have a directly elected mayor.
e: True — for example, London has a directly elected mayor.

q: Since 1997, some powers have been given to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. What is this called?
e: Devolution means the national parliament has given some powers to the parliaments and assemblies of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

q: Where is the Scottish Parliament?
e: The Scottish Parliament sits in Edinburgh at Holyrood.

q: How are members of the Scottish Parliament (MSPs) elected?
o: By a form of proportional representation
By first past the post only
They are appointed by the First Minister
e: MSPs are elected by a form of proportional representation.

q: Where does the Welsh Parliament (Senedd) meet?
o: In the Senedd building in Cardiff Bay
e: The Welsh Senedd meets in Cardiff Bay.
x: Today: the Welsh Assembly has been called the Senedd (Welsh Parliament) since 2020.

q: Where does the Northern Ireland Assembly meet?
e: The Northern Ireland Assembly meets at Stormont in Belfast.

q: Which agreement led to the setting up of the Northern Ireland Assembly?
e: The Northern Ireland Assembly was set up after the Good Friday Agreement in 1998.

q: The Northern Ireland Assembly has been suspended several times.
e: True — it has been suspended a few times, and powers returned to the UK government.

q: What is the name of the official report of everything said in Parliament?
e: Proceedings in Parliament are published in Hansard and broadcast on TV.

q: In the UK, the press is free from government control.
e: True — the UK has a free press. Newspaper owners and editors may hold strong political opinions.

q: TV and radio must give balanced coverage of political parties.
e: True — by law, radio and TV coverage of political parties must be balanced.

q: What is the minimum age to vote in UK Parliament elections?
e: The voting age for UK Parliament elections is 18.
x: Some elections in Scotland and Wales let people vote at 16.

q: Which TWO groups can vote in all UK public elections if they live in the UK and are 18 or over?
e: UK, Irish and eligible Commonwealth citizens aged 18 or over who live here can vote in all public elections.

q: What must you do before you can vote?
e: You must have your name on the electoral register. You can register online.

q: Where can you get a voter registration form?
o: From your local council's electoral registration office, or register online
e: Contact your local council's electoral registration office, or register online.

q: Where do people go to vote in elections?
e: You vote at a polling station, usually in a public building such as a school.

q: What are the opening hours of polling stations on election day?
e: Polls are open from 7 am to 10 pm.

q: You can vote by post instead of going to a polling station.
e: True — you can apply for a postal vote.

q: The vote is secret — no one can make you say who you voted for.
e: True — the UK has a secret ballot.

q: Which TWO groups of people cannot stand for Parliament?
e: Most citizens aged 18 or over can stand. Exceptions include members of the armed forces, civil servants and people with certain criminal convictions.

q: How can you contact your MP?
o: By letter, phone or email, or at a local "surgery"
e: Many MPs hold regular local "surgeries" where constituents can meet them.

q: Members of the public can watch debates in the Houses of Parliament.
e: True — you can watch from the public galleries. Entry is free.

q: What is the Commonwealth?
o: A voluntary association of countries, most of which were once part of the British Empire
A trading group of European countries
The countries ruled by the UK today
e: Commonwealth countries work together towards shared goals in democracy and development.

q: What is the Council of Europe?
o: An organisation that protects human rights and created the European Convention on Human Rights
The government of the European Union
e: The Council of Europe is separate from the EU. It developed the European Convention on Human Rights.

q: Which international organisation was set up after the Second World War to prevent war and promote peace?
e: The UN was set up after the Second World War. The UK is a member.

q: The UK is one of how many permanent members of the UN Security Council?
e: The UK is one of five permanent members of the UN Security Council.

q: What is NATO?
o: A group of European and North American countries that have agreed to help each other if attacked
e: NATO members agree to help each other if attacked.

q: Which TWO are examples of criminal offences?
e: Criminal law covers crimes. Disputes about goods or housing are usually civil law.

q: Which TWO are examples of civil law?
o: Housing disputes between landlords and tenants
e: Civil law settles disputes between people, such as consumer rights, housing and employment.

q: It is a criminal offence to smoke in public places.
e: True — it is against the law to smoke in almost every enclosed public place.

q: It is legal to buy alcohol for someone under 18.
e: False — it is a criminal offence to buy alcohol for someone under 18.

q: What is the minimum age to buy tobacco products?
e: It is illegal to sell tobacco products to anyone under 18.

q: Which TWO are duties of the police?
e: The police protect life and property, keep the peace, and prevent and detect crime.

q: Who supports the police by patrolling streets and dealing with anti-social behaviour?
e: PCSOs patrol the streets and work with the public.

q: Since 2012, who has been elected in England and Wales to make sure the police are effective?
e: Since November 2012, people have voted for Police and Crime Commissioners.

q: The police must obey the law and must not misuse their authority.
e: True — the police are servants of the public and must act within the law.

q: Who hears minor criminal cases in magistrates' courts in England and Wales?
e: Most minor criminal cases are dealt with in a magistrates' court.

q: Magistrates are usually paid and have legal qualifications.
e: False — magistrates usually work unpaid and do not need legal qualifications. They receive training.

q: Where are serious criminal offences tried in England, Wales and Northern Ireland?
o: In a Crown Court, in front of a judge and a jury
e: Serious offences are tried in a Crown Court with a judge and jury.

q: How many people are on a jury in England, Wales and Northern Ireland?
e: A jury in England, Wales and Northern Ireland has 12 members of the public.

q: How many people are on a jury in Scotland?
e: In Scotland a jury has 15 members.

q: In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, which court hears cases for young people aged 10 to 17?
e: Young people aged 10 to 17 are tried in a youth court.

q: What is Scotland's system for dealing with children and young people accused of an offence?
e: Scotland uses the Children's Hearings System.

q: Which court deals with civil disputes such as debts and personal injury in England and Wales?
e: County Courts deal with a wide range of civil disputes.

q: What is the small claims procedure for claims under £10,000 in England and Wales?
o: An informal way to settle small disputes without a lawyer
A criminal court for minor theft
e: The small claims procedure helps people settle minor disputes without spending lots of money on a lawyer.

q: In a criminal trial, a jury has to decide whether the accused is guilty or not guilty.
e: True — the judge then decides the penalty.

q: What is the European Convention on Human Rights?
o: A list of rights, including the right to life and a fair trial, that the UK has signed
A law made by the EU
e: The UK signed the Convention. Most of it is part of UK law through the Human Rights Act 1998.

q: Which TWO rights are protected by the European Convention on Human Rights?
o: Freedom of thought, conscience and religion
e: The Convention includes the right to life, freedom from torture and slavery, a fair trial, and freedom of thought and expression.

q: Which law makes it illegal to discriminate in many areas of life in England, Wales and Scotland?
e: The Equality Act 2010 protects people from discrimination at work and elsewhere.

q: Violence in the home, including against a partner, is a serious crime.
e: True — anyone who is violent towards their partner can be prosecuted.

q: Female genital mutilation (FGM) is a crime in the UK.
e: True — it is illegal to carry out FGM or arrange for it to be done, in the UK or abroad.

q: What is a forced marriage?
o: A marriage where one or both parties do not or cannot agree to it
A marriage arranged by families with both people's agreement
A marriage at a register office
e: Forced marriage is illegal. Courts can issue Forced Marriage Protection Orders.

q: An arranged marriage where both people agree is the same as a forced marriage.
e: False — in an arranged marriage both people agree. A forced marriage is without their consent and is illegal.

q: What do you pay income tax on?
o: Your earnings, including wages, self-employed profits and some other income
e: Income tax is paid on earnings, profits, some benefits, pensions and income from savings and property.

q: How is income tax usually paid by people who work for an employer?
o: Automatically from their wages through PAYE
They pay it in cash once a year
They pay it at the post office
e: Most people pay income tax through Pay As You Earn (PAYE).

q: Who must pay their own tax through self assessment?
o: Only people who work for the government
e: Self-employed people pay their own tax through self assessment.

q: What is National Insurance used for?
o: Paying for state benefits and services such as the State Pension and the NHS
e: National Insurance contributions help pay for the State Pension and the NHS.

q: Almost everybody in the UK who is in paid work, including self-employed people, must pay National Insurance contributions.
e: True — people who don't pay enough may not get certain benefits or a full State Pension.

q: What is the minimum age to drive a car or motorcycle in the UK?
e: You must be at least 17 to drive a car or motorcycle and have a driving licence.

q: What happens to your driving licence when you reach 70?
o: You must renew it, and then every three years
You must take a new driving test
e: A licence is valid until you are 70. After that it must be renewed every three years.

q: It is a criminal offence to drive without insurance.
e: True — all drivers must have insurance.

q: What test must vehicles over three years old pass every year?
e: Vehicles over three years old must have an MOT test every year.

q: Which of these is a way you can help your community?
e: Volunteering and working with your community is part of being a good citizen.

q: Which TWO are good ways to help the environment?
e: Recycling and using public transport help the environment.

q: Dropping litter in the street can result in a fine.
e: True — it is a criminal offence to drop litter.

q: What is jury service?
o: A duty to serve on a jury if you are called
e: Anyone on the electoral register may be chosen at random to serve on a jury.

q: Anyone on the electoral register may be asked to serve on a jury.
e: True — people on the electoral register can be called at random. Some people are not allowed to serve.

q: How can people help their children's school?
o: By becoming a school governor (school board member in Scotland)
e: Parents can volunteer as school governors or school board members.

q: You can register as an organ donor.
e: True — many people choose to donate organs after they die.
x: Today: across the UK, most adults are now considered donors unless they opt out.

q: In an emergency, which numbers can you call for police, fire or ambulance?
e: In an emergency call 999 or 112.

q: What does the national anthem ask for the monarch?
o: That God will save and protect them
That they will win every war
That they will live in London
That they will choose the government
e: The national anthem is "God Save the King" (or Queen).

q: It is legal for a man to force his wife to have sex.
e: False — it is a crime for a man to force his wife to have sex.

q: Which of these is a way to take part in politics?
e: You can join a political party, help with campaigns or stand for office.

q: People can visit the Scottish Parliament, the Senedd and the Northern Ireland Assembly.
e: True — each has a public gallery or visitor arrangements.
